narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and unfortunately, the model predicted a 57% probability that you would not pass — a slim but decisive margin that led to your application being rejected. While this is not an overwhelming prediction of failure, it reflects enough concern about your current academic profile that the system flagged your application as high-risk. Understanding why this happened, and what could change it, is the first step toward strengthening your path forward.

To help explain this decision, the model was tested against a series of "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile where certain factors were different enough to flip the prediction from "will fail" to "will pass." These counterfactual scenarios are not judgments about who you are, but rather a map of where the model sees the greatest opportunity for improvement. Ten such scenarios were generated for your profile, and the results were remarkably consistent in pointing to a single factor as the key to changing the outcome.

Across all ten alternative scenarios, the only feature that ever changed was your LSAT score — it changed in 100% of cases, while every other factor in your profile, including your first- and third-year academic decile rankings, your family income, your undergraduate GPA, and your part-time enrollment status, remained unchanged in every scenario. This is a striking finding: the model is essentially telling you that your LSAT score is the single most critical lever in this decision. On average, the scenarios that would flip the prediction required your LSAT score to increase by approximately 12 points, from your current score of 25 to around 37 — which, notably, is almost exactly the average LSAT score among students who successfully passed the bar exam in the dataset.

Your current LSAT score of 25 sits significantly below that average of 37, and this gap appears to be the dominant concern driving the model's prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.40 is also below the average of 3.24 among students who passed, and your first-year academic decile ranking of 1 is well below the average of approximately 6 among successful students — but the model's counterfactuals suggest that improving your LSAT score alone could be sufficient to change the outcome, without requiring changes to those other factors. This does not mean those other areas are unimportant to your overall preparation, but it does mean the model weighs your LSAT performance most heavily when assessing bar exam readiness.

As a part-time student, you are already in a smaller group — only about 7% of students who passed the bar exam in this dataset were enrolled part-time — so your path may require more deliberate preparation than a full-time student's. The most actionable step you can take is to invest seriously in LSAT preparation, with the goal of reaching a score in the mid-to-upper 30s. A 12-point improvement is achievable with structured study, practice exams, and potentially professional tutoring, and based on the model's analysis, reaching that threshold could be the difference between rejection and approval.
